```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Each render rebuilds the results from the supplied source. It never installs
# packages, changes raw data, contacts GitHub or downloads new observations.
roots <- c(".", "..")
roots <- roots[file.exists(file.path(roots, "scripts/predictive_models.R"))]
if (!length(roots)) stop("Open this file inside the complete project repository.")
ROOT <- normalizePath(roots[1])
if (dir.exists(file.path(ROOT, ".r-library"))) {
  .libPaths(c(file.path(ROOT, ".r-library"), .libPaths()))
}
options(warn = 2, knitr.kable.NA = "--")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
source(file.path(ROOT, "scripts/descriptive_followup.R"), local = TRUE)
source(file.path(ROOT, "scripts/predictive_models.R"), local = TRUE)
SOURCE <- file.path(ROOT, "data",
  "business-establishments-and-jobs-data-by-business-size-and-anzsic.csv")
OUT <- file.path(ROOT, "outputs/tables/final")
desc <- run_followup(SOURCE, file.path(OUT, "descriptive"))
models <- run_predictive(SOURCE, file.path(OUT, "predictive"))
sensitivity <- pred_evaluate_sensitivity(SOURCE, models, file.path(OUT, "scope_sensitivity"))
m <- desc$metrics
selected <- models$selected_configuration
test <- models$test_metrics
nb <- filter(test, model == "No change")
error_summary <- filter(models$error_concentration_summary, model == "No change")
cover <- filter(models$comparison_coverage, stage == "Held-out test")
cases <- desc$tables$case_studies
screen <- desc$tables$priority_screen_summary
case_row <- function(industry_name) {
  row <- filter(cases, industry == industry_name)
  if (nrow(row) != 1) stop("Expected case study missing from the ranked shortlist.")
  row
}
professional <- case_row("Professional, Scientific and Technical Services")
finance <- case_row("Financial and Insurance Services")
admin <- case_row("Administrative and Support Services")
health <- case_row("Health Care and Social Assistance")
construction <- case_row("Construction")
num <- function(x) scales::comma(x, accuracy = 1)
percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", x)
table_out <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, digits = 2, ...)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE, error = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10.5, fig.height = 6, dpi = 160, out.width = "100%")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom"))
```

# 1. The question and the answer

**Research question:** Which precinct–industry groups show the greatest evidence
of persistent SME weakness, and where should the City prioritise further support?

The Lord Mayor needs evidence to focus attention across a city with uneven
business recovery. A rising city total can hide industries that continue to
lose business locations. We examine changes across precincts and industries
from 2002 to 2024, then compare the remaining gap from 2019 with recent change
from 2022. This turns the broad recovery question into a specific review list.

We use **Small and Medium establishments (1–199 jobs)** throughout. An
establishment is a business location. One company may operate several locations.

Three findings matter:

- **Recovery remains incomplete.** The city had 13,054 SME establishments in
  2024, `r percent(abs(m$city_gap_pct))` below 2019. The gain of
  `r num(m$city_recent_gain)` since 2022 offset
  `r percent(m$share_of_2019_to_2022_loss_offset_pct)` of the earlier loss.
- **The CBD and hospitality account for much of the recent increase.** The CBD
  contributed `r percent(m$cbd_share_of_recent_city_gain_pct)` of the city net gain.
  Accommodation and Food Services contributed
  `r percent(m$hospitality_share_of_city_net_gain_pct)`. These describe different
  breakdowns of the same city total and should not be added together.
- **Five CBD groups make the remaining weakness concrete.** Professional
  services, finance, administrative support, health care and construction have
  the largest 2019 shortfalls among groups that also declined after 2022.
  Together, they account for `r num(m$case_shortfall)` fewer establishments than
  in 2019 and a further loss of `r num(m$case_recent_loss)` after 2022.

The recommendations follow these observed patterns. Forecast comparisons help
explain why we have not used a model-generated ranking of future recovery.

# 2. What we did with the data

## 2.1 Coverage, variables and unit of analysis

The City of Melbourne's Census of Land Use and Employment (CLUE) supplies two
files covering 2002–2024. The aggregated file has **`r num(m$source_rows)` rows
and `r m$source_columns` variables**: census year, precinct, ANZSIC industry
division, business size, establishment count and job count. A row is a
year–precinct–industry–size combination containing a count of establishments.
It does not represent an individual business.

Selecting Small and Medium categories retains **`r num(m$selected_source_rows)`
source rows**, spanning `r m$source_years` census years, `r m$precincts` precincts
and `r m$industries` industry divisions. We add the published Small and Medium
counts within each year–precinct–industry group. For example, “CBD professional
services in 2024” is one analytical group, containing 1,338 establishments.
Large and non-employing businesses are outside the main population.

The address file contains **413,550 records and 12 fields**, including census
year, property identifiers, address, industry and coordinates. It supports
all-size count checks. It has no business-size field, so we do not use it to
identify individual SMEs or join business-level attributes onto the SME counts.

## 2.2 Preparation and data quality

We standardised names and types, checked the grouping keys for duplicates,
and tested establishment counts for missing, negative or non-integer values.
The aggregated file passed these checks. Precinct and industry totals were
reconciled to the city total after selecting SMEs.

Job counts are missing in **`r num(m$missing_job_rows)` aggregated rows
(`r percent(m$missing_job_pct)`)**, all containing two or fewer establishments.
This is consistent with confidentiality suppression. Their establishment
counts are available, so we retain the rows and leave jobs missing. Jobs are
not an outcome or predictor in this analysis.

The address file includes **68,299 Vacant Space records across all years**.
We retain the original records and separate this recorded category when
checking operating-establishment totals. The aggregated SME file has no
vacancy category. This step does not identify unrecorded closures or correct
the survey cycle. The [data audit](01_descriptive_analytics.html) records the
checks and remaining differences between the two sources.

## 2.3 Why these years and comparisons?

Two-year-or-longer comparisons follow CLUE's two-year property survey cycle.
We use **2019 as the pre-pandemic reference, 2022 as the recent recovery
starting point and 2024 as the latest supplied year**. The city series gives
longer-term context: 11,271 SMEs in 2002, 15,515 in 2017 and 15,506 in 2019.
The near-flat 2017–2019 comparison helps distinguish the later shortfall from
a long-running city-wide decline. These comparisons describe changes around
the pandemic without estimating its causal effect.

An absent source combination stays unknown. The three-year descriptive
screen has `r screen$complete_three_year_groups` complete groups out of
`r screen$groups_in_any_reference_year` observed in at least one reference year.
The other `r screen$incomplete_groups` cannot be classified by that screen.
We report counts for small groups and withhold percentage comparisons where
the relevant starting count is below 100. This is our reporting choice, not a
CLUE rule. Small groups remain in city totals.

# 3. Where recovery is happening

## 3.1 The city is growing again, but remains below 2019

```{r city-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6}
desc$figures$city_recovery
```

The count fell by `r num(15506 - 12571)` between 2019 and 2022, then rose by
`r num(m$city_recent_gain)` by 2024. The remaining gap is
`r num(m$city_remaining_shortfall)` establishments. This is net change in
establishment counts, not a count of closures or a causal estimate of COVID-19.

## 3.2 The CBD has the largest gap and the largest recent gain

```{r precinct-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8}
desc$figures$precinct_changes
```

All `r m$precincts_below_2019` precincts remained below their 2019 counts.
`r m$precincts_increasing_since_2022` increased after 2022.
The CBD accounts for `r percent(m$cbd_share_of_remaining_city_shortfall_pct)`
of the remaining city shortfall and added `r num(m$cbd_recent_gain)` recently.
Large remaining losses and recent improvement can occur in the same precinct.

## 3.3 Hospitality gains coexist with continuing service-sector losses

```{r industry-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8}
desc$figures$industry_recent_change
```

Accommodation and Food Services added `r num(m$hospitality_recent_gain)`
establishments city-wide. Industry gains totalled `r num(m$gross_industry_gains)`;
industry losses totalled `r num(abs(m$gross_industry_losses))`, leaving a net
gain of `r num(m$city_recent_gain)`.

Within the CBD, hospitality increased by 180, while Professional, Scientific
and Technical Services fell by 45. CBD professional services also had the
largest precinct–industry shortfall from 2019, at 450. This makes the industry
breakdown more informative than calling the whole CBD “recovered” or “declining”.

# 4. Five groups that explain the priority list

## 4.1 From 64 flagged groups to five specific cases

Our screen asks two questions: **Was the 2024 count below 2019? Did it fall
again between 2022 and 2024?** `r screen$groups_meeting_screen` of the
`r screen$complete_three_year_groups` comparable precinct–industry groups meet
both conditions. Each group counts business locations in one industry within
one precinct.

For closer review, we rank those groups by their **absolute 2019–2024
shortfall and select the five largest**. All five are in the CBD. The rule
favours gaps affecting more establishments; it does not estimate which policy
would deliver the greatest benefit. The five account for
`r percent(100 * m$case_shortfall / m$city_remaining_shortfall)` of the city's
remaining net shortfall. Other groups still matter: the full screen is exported,
including `r screen$screened_with_small_baseline` groups with a baseline below
100 in at least one comparison.

```{r five-cases-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7}
desc$figures$priority_cases
```

```{r five-cases-counts, echo=FALSE}
table_out(cases |> transmute(`Industry (all Melbourne CBD)` = industry,
  `2019` = num(n_2019), `2022` = num(n_2022), `2024` = num(n_2024),
  `2019-2024 change` = percent(gap_pct), `2022-2024 change` = percent(recent_pct)))
```

## 4.2 What each case tells the City

**Professional, Scientific and Technical Services: the largest remaining gap.**
The count fell from `r num(professional$n_2019)` to `r num(professional$n_2024)`,
leaving `r num(professional$shortfall_count)` fewer establishments than in 2019.
It lost a further `r num(abs(professional$recent_change))` after 2022, the largest
recent decline among these five groups. Its scale makes it the clearest starting
point for investigating weaker CBD business presence. Growth in CBD hospitality
does not offset this industry's loss of locations.

**Financial and Insurance Services: a second substantial service-sector gap.**
Finance fell from `r num(finance$n_2019)` to `r num(finance$n_2024)` establishments,
a `r percent(abs(finance$gap_pct))` reduction. The additional loss of
`r num(abs(finance$recent_change))` after 2022 shows that the earlier shortfall
was still widening. Together, finance and professional services place much of
the remaining weakness in the CBD's service economy.

**Administrative and Support Services: the deepest proportional decline.**
This group fell from `r num(admin$n_2019)` to `r num(admin$n_2024)`, down
`r percent(abs(admin$gap_pct))`. It also lost `r num(abs(admin$recent_change))`
establishments after 2022 (`r percent(abs(admin$recent_pct))`). Its smaller size
than professional services should not obscure the much larger proportional
loss. Both scale and recent direction support keeping it near the top of the
City's review list.

**Health Care and Social Assistance: a historical gap with little recent movement.**
The count remains `r num(health$shortfall_count)` below 2019, but fell only
`r num(abs(health$recent_change))` after 2022 (`r percent(abs(health$recent_pct))`).
It qualifies because the screen uses direction, with no minimum decline
threshold. The recent change provides a weaker urgency signal than in the
other four cases. This is a useful distinction when deciding which groups
need the closest attention.

**Construction: a smaller group with the sharpest recent percentage decline.**
Construction fell from `r num(construction$n_2019)` to
`r num(construction$n_2024)` establishments. Its loss of
`r num(abs(construction$recent_change))` since 2022 represents
`r percent(abs(construction$recent_pct))`, the largest recent percentage
decline among the five. The count measures construction business locations
in the CBD; it does not measure construction output or the number of projects.

# 5. What prediction added

We tested whether historical counts could improve forecasts of each group's
next two-year change. The comparison used a no-change benchmark, multiple
linear regression, a pruned regression tree and gradient boosting. Current
count, its log transform, previous two-year change, precinct and industry were
the predictors. Even-year observations provide consistent two-year steps
aligned with the survey cycle.

Four expanding-window validation periods selected settings using mean absolute
error (MAE). Outcomes from 2024 were excluded from model selection. Every
selected model was then evaluated on the same `r cover$comparison_cells`
groups for 2022–2024.

```{r model-summary, echo=FALSE}
table_out(test |> transmute(Model = model,
  `MAE (establishments per group)` = mae))
```

No change predicts that a group's count stays at its starting level. It had the
lowest average error among the tested methods. In the evaluation sample,
`r percent(100 * error_summary$actual_change_within_5_share)` of groups changed
by five establishments or fewer, which helps explain why the simple benchmark
was competitive. That does not imply that the city stopped changing.

The baseline missed the matched sample's net increase of
`r num(nb$actual_total_change)` establishments, and its error was much larger
for large groups. We therefore make no model-based 2026 forecast. **Observed
shortfalls and recent changes support the recommendations.** Full model
settings, sample coverage and error diagnostics are in Appendix A.

# 6. Recommendations and conclusion

**Focus the first review on CBD professional services, finance and administrative
support.** Together they have `r num(sum(c(professional$shortfall_count,
finance$shortfall_count, admin$shortfall_count)))` fewer establishments than in
2019 and lost a further `r num(abs(sum(c(professional$recent_change,
finance$recent_change, admin$recent_change))))` after 2022. They combine the
largest historical gaps with continuing losses. This gives the City a specific
set of industries to consider when setting SME support priorities.

**Keep construction and health care distinct within that review.** Construction
shows a stronger recent decline relative to its size. Health care's recent
count is nearly unchanged despite its historical gap. A single “declining”
label would conceal that difference.

**Use the precinct–industry breakdown when discussing recovery.** The CBD added
245 SMEs overall, including 180 in hospitality, while the five reviewed
industries lost 107. City growth and continuing local weakness coexist. The
same breakdown should guide consideration of the remaining screened groups
outside these five cases.

The study identifies where business presence has weakened and how the pattern
differs across groups. Choosing a particular grant, incentive or funding amount
requires evidence on business needs and intervention costs that CLUE does not
provide. Policy implementation schedules and programme evaluation are outside
this report's scope.

# Appendix A. Predictive methods and diagnostics

## A.1 Target, predictors and models

For each precinct–industry group:

**Target change = establishments at t+2 − establishments at t.**

For example, a count of 100 rising to 108 gives a target of +8. No change
predicts a target of zero, equivalent to predicting that 100 establishments
remain. Its absolute error in this example is 8.

The fitted models use five predictors available at the starting date: the
current count, log(1 + current count), the previous two-year change, precinct
and industry. The log term allows OLS to describe a curved size relationship
without forcing the effect of size to be purely proportional.

- **No change:** a simple benchmark with no fitted coefficients.
- **Multiple linear regression (OLS):** a transparent additive relationship
  between the predictors and the next change.
- **Pruned regression tree:** thresholds and interactions, with pruning chosen
  from historical validation rather than random cross-validation.
- **Gradient boosting:** a small ensemble of shallow regression trees, tested
  to see whether added flexibility improves prediction.

Every method is assessed on identical cells. Predicted changes are bounded
below by minus the starting count, so a forecast cannot imply a negative number
of establishments. Predictions are not rounded before scoring.

## A.2 Keep later outcomes out of model selection

We grow the training window forward through time. For a prediction made at
year t, training can use only changes whose **outcome year is at or before t**.
The train/test separation applies to time, not a random selection of rows.

```{r timeline, echo=FALSE}
timing <- models$validation_predictions |>
  distinct(origin_year, target_year, train_first_origin, train_last_origin,
           train_last_target, training_rows) |>
  transmute(`Training origins` = paste(train_first_origin, train_last_origin, sep = "-"),
    `Last observed training outcome` = train_last_target,
    `Validation period` = paste(origin_year, target_year, sep = "-"),
    `Training rows` = training_rows)
table_out(timing)
```

The tree grid tests pruning parameters 0.001, 0.01 and 0.05, with minimum leaf
sizes of 5 or 10. Boosting tests depths 1 or 2 and 100 or 300 trees, with a
learning rate of 0.03. No random subsampling is used.

We average the four validation MAEs, giving each historical period equal
weight. That selects a configuration within each model family and an overall
model **before** the 2022–2024 evaluation. The selected model is
**`r selected$model`**. These are reconstructed historical tests using the
supplied data vintage, not a prospective test on newly observed outcomes.

## A.3 Results on the 2022–2024 evaluation

```{r accuracy-table, echo=FALSE}
table_out(test |> transmute(Model = model, Cells = n, MAE = mae, RMSE = rmse,
  `Mean error` = bias, `Selected before test` = selected_before_test))
```

MAE is the average absolute error, in establishments per group. RMSE gives
large errors more weight. Mean error is predicted minus actual change: negative
values indicate underprediction.

```{r model-accuracy, echo=FALSE}
accuracy_plot <- ggplot(test, aes(mae, reorder(model, -mae))) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = selected_before_test), width = .6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", mae)), hjust = -.2, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#187F86", "FALSE" = "#A7B6C2")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, max(test$mae) * 1.2)) +
  labs(title = "No change has the lowest average error in the final evaluation",
    subtitle = "2022-2024; the same 207 precinct-industry groups for every model.",
    x = "Mean absolute error (establishments per group)", y = NULL,
    caption = "Group 10 rebuild from supplied CLUE data. Models selected using earlier periods.")
accuracy_plot
```

The evaluation includes `r cover$comparison_cells` of
`r cover$published_origin_cells` published starting groups and
`r percent(100 * cover$share_of_origin_establishments)` of their establishments.
The matched sample gained `r num(nb$actual_total_change)` establishments, compared
with `r num(m$city_recent_gain)` for the city. Coverage tables account for the
difference; it is not silently treated as zero.

The baseline wins on test MAE and RMSE in this rebuild. Historical validation
RMSE and MAE do not always rank models in the same order; the model-selection
rule was MAE throughout. The complete validation leaderboard is exported.

## A.4 Why no change performs well, and where it is weak

`r percent(100 * error_summary$actual_change_within_5_share)` of evaluation groups
changed by five establishments or fewer. `r percent(100 * error_summary$origin_count_under_20_share)`
started with fewer than 20 establishments. Predicting zero can keep errors
small across many such groups without estimating extra relationships.

That is a pattern in the evaluation sample, not proof that every group is
stable. Only `r percent(100 * error_summary$actual_zero_change_share)` had exactly
zero change. Large changes still matter.

```{r size-errors, echo=FALSE}
size_errors <- models$subgroups |>
  filter(model == "No change", grouping == "origin_size_band") |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("0-19", "20-99", "100+")))
size_plot <- ggplot(size_errors, aes(group, mae)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#253F57", width = .55) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f\n(n = %d)", mae, n)), vjust = -.3, size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .2))) +
  labs(title = "Baseline errors are much larger in large groups",
    subtitle = "2022-2024 no-change predictions, grouped by 2022 count.",
    x = "SME establishments in a precinct-industry group in 2022",
    y = "Mean absolute error (establishments per group)")
size_plot
```

The ten largest errors account for
`r percent(100 * error_summary$top_10_cells_error_share)` of total absolute error.
The no-change prediction misses the matched sample's net gain of
`r num(nb$actual_total_change)`. We therefore use it as a benchmark, while
using observed local gaps and recent changes to support investigation priorities.
A zero-change forecast cannot rank which groups will recover fastest.

## A.5 What changes when non-employing establishments are included?

```{r scope-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
table_out(sensitivity$common_cell_scope_comparison |>
  transmute(Scope = if_else(stage == "Held-out test", "Small + Medium",
    "Small + Medium + Non employing"),
    Model = model, `Matched cells` = n, MAE = mae, RMSE = rmse,
    `Observed net change` = actual_total_change))
```

This check holds each model family's main-analysis configuration fixed and compares identical
group keys. It changes the population, so its counts and error sizes should
not replace the main results. The separate data audit compares descriptive
results under both definitions.

# Appendix B. Supplementary industry-mix comparison

We compare each precinct with the **same industries elsewhere in the city**.
For each matched industry, we multiply the local starting count by the
rest-of-city industry's observed growth factor. We then sum the comparison
counts over the same cells as the observed counts.

```{r industry-mix-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8}
desc$figures$industry_mix_comparison
```

A negative value means local growth was below that descriptive comparison.
It suggests a question for local investigation without estimating the effect
of a precinct, COVID-19 or a policy. It is supplementary to the five-case
selection and does not determine that ranking.

The chart requires at least 95% count coverage in both years and a starting
count of 100. These are our reporting thresholds. The exported tables also
repeat the comparison after requiring 100 establishments in each rest-of-city
reference industry, to check sensitivity to small reference groups.

# Appendix C. Audit trail and reproduction

The report is generated from R Markdown, which runs the calculations and
inserts the resulting tables and figures. The supplied CSV files remain
unchanged. Source checksums, package versions and test results are saved with
the analysis outputs.

Run from the repository root:

```sh
Rscript scripts/install_dependencies.R
Rscript scripts/run_final_analysis.R
```

The first command installs missing packages once. The second runs both test
suites and rebuilds the data audit, final analysis, charts and exported results.
No packages or source datasets are downloaded during analysis.

The code checks duplicate keys, invalid counts, source-file hashes, missing
cells, reconciliation, identical evaluation samples, exact two-year alignment,
and temporal leakage. A test changes the held-out outcomes and confirms that
all four models' predictions remain unchanged.

Key files:

- `scripts/descriptive_followup.R`: counts, contributions, industry-mix comparison
  and observed review lists.
- `scripts/predictive_models.R`: panel construction, validation, fitting and errors.
- `tests/test_final_analysis.R`: independent calculations and failure-case tests.
- `outputs/tables/final/`: every score, prediction, exclusion, setting and figure.

The report uses the supplied 2002–2024 snapshot. It does not estimate individual
business survival, policy effects, employment growth or the causal effect of
COVID-19. There are only four validation periods and one final evaluation
period. The error rankings do not establish statistical significance.

## Sources and assistance

City of Melbourne: [aggregated CLUE dataset](https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/business-establishments-and-jobs-data-by-business-size-and-anzsic-in-small-areas)

The supplied files, rather than live downloads, are used here.

naive benchmarks, forecast errors and rolling-origin evaluation.
[rpart documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rpart) and
[gbm documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/package=gbm) describe the fitted tree methods.

Claude assisted with code review as reported by the group. Codex assisted with
code, tests, charts and wording. The group is responsible for reviewing the
analysis and the final submission.
